one_liner: Research CUDA hash-based SpGEMM (C = A*B, CSR, FP64) for V100; paper reports 7.35x average over cuSPARSE.
what_it_does: Computes the sparse-sparse product C = A*B for CSR matrices with double values and 32-bit int indices on one NVIDIA GPU, using the usual two-pass flow: count each output row's nonzeros (symbolic), allocate C, then fill values (numeric). It is research code with a driver main(), not a packaged library. The entry point is opsparse(A, B, C, meta, timing), which takes the repo's own CSR and Meta classes, so it is not a drop-in replacement for cusparseSpGEMM. The repo also bundles copies of nsparse and spECK, plus a cuSPARSE driver, as comparison harnesses.
how_it_is_fast: Rows are binned by an upper bound on their output size (8 bins, ranges sized for about 1.2x hash-table headroom). Each bin then runs a kernel sized to it: a partial warp of 4 threads per row with a 32-slot table for tiny rows, thread-block shared-memory hash tables of 512 to 8192 slots, a 96 KB dynamic-shared-memory kernel, and a global-memory hash fallback for rows that overflow. The hash tables use linear probing with atomicCAS and a multiplicative hash (column * 107), and each row's output is put in column order by an in-block counting sort. Per the paper abstract, the other gains come from fewer hash-table accesses, packing all metadata into one combined allocation, and overlapping cudaMalloc of C with kernel execution across 8 streams.
when_to_use: Repeated SpGEMM (A*A, A*P, Galerkin products in AMG setup, graph algorithms) on a Volta-class GPU, where cuSPARSE SpGEMM time dominates
FP64 CSR matrices with 32-bit indices and up to about 2^31 nonzeros in C
As a reference implementation or starting point when writing your own binned hash SpGEMM, since the kernels are short and readable
Benchmark studies: the repo already wires cuSPARSE, nsparse and spECK drivers to the same matrix loader
when_not_to_use: On A100/H100-class GPUs, where independent results put it behind spECK: Ocean (ICS 2026, 337 matrices on A100) reports 2.6x over OpSparse but only 1.4x over spECK
When you need FP32, complex, 64-bit indices, or a C = alpha*A*B + beta*C API: values are hard-wired to double and indices to int
Production code that needs a maintained library: 9 commits, last one 2022-08-23, no tests, and the result check against cuSPARSE is commented out in the drivers
Non-NVIDIA hardware or non-x86 hosts: CUDA only, and the timer reads rdtsc and the CPUID leaf 0x16 base frequency
Turing-class GPUs (64 KB shared-memory limit per block): the large-row kernels request 98,304 bytes of dynamic shared memory

integration.dependencies: CUDA toolkit (tested 11.2) with cuSPARSE and CUB, OpenMP (host flop count), CUDA samples headers on the include path
integration.min_toolchain: nvcc from CUDA 11.x (tested 11.2) with g++; Makefile hard-codes -arch=compute_70 -code=sm_70
integration.platforms: NVIDIA GPUs, sm_70 (V100) as shipped; x86-64 host for the rdtsc-based timer
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each call creates and destroys its own 8 CUDA streams and device buffers through a Meta object, so share neither Meta nor CSR objects across host threads
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — computes the same product as cusparseSpGEMM but through its own CSR/Meta classes and an opsparse(A, B, C, meta, timing) call; you would wrap or extract the kernels

gotchas: The Makefile embeds only sm_70 SASS (no PTX), so the binaries will not run on Ampere or Hopper until you change GENCODE
Meta::release frees host memory from malloc with delete[] (combined_mem), which is undefined behaviour; fix it before embedding
CUDA errors throw std::exception after printing; there is no error-code API

The cuSPARSE driver times cusparseCreate/cusparseDestroy and buffer allocation inside every call (the OpSparse timing also includes its own allocations), which can inflate the cuSPARSE baseline on small matrices
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick spECK (GPUPeople/spECK) by default: on the third-party sets found (Ocean on A100; the ACM study cited in the record's caveats, which puts OpSparse at 4.91x and spECK at 5.67x average over cuSPARSE) it is as fast or faster. OpSparse is the more compact code to adapt. TileSpGEMM reports beating spECK on 94 of 142 matrices, and Kokkos Kernels SpGEMM is the maintained, portable choice.
verified_claims_summary: Per the IEEE Access 2022 abstract (search snippets; the paper was not opened), on 26 common SuiteSparse matrices on a Tesla V100 with CUDA 11.2, OpSparse averages 7.35x (up to 27.8x) over cuSPARSE SpGEMM, 1.43x (up to 1.81x) over nsparse and 1.52x (up to 2.04x) over spECK, in FP64. The repo holds the harness (reg_opsparse, reg_cusparse, nvcc -O3 sm_70) but no result files, and later third-party studies find smaller margins or spECK ahead.
status_note: Abandoned since August 2022 (9 commits, no issues filed); MIT-licensed, including the bundled nsparse and spECK copies, and small enough to vendor, but last known to work only with CUDA 11.2 on V100.
sources_read: WebSearch snippets: arXiv 2206.07244 abstract; Ocean ICS 2026 (arXiv 2604.19004) abstract
